newsitem.title: POLAND: FORECAST - POLISH 1997 GDP SEEN UP 5.4 PCT - THINKTANK.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - POLISH 1997 GDP SEEN UP 5.4 PCT - THINKTANK.

text.p: Poland's economy is estimated to have grown by 5.6 percent in 1996, down from seven percent in 1995, and to slow down to 5.4 percent in 1997 and 4.8 percent in 1998, an independent think-tank said on Thursday.

The private Gdansk Institute for Market Economy Research (IBnGR) said that year-on-year inflation in December 1997 was likely to ease to 15-16 percent, rather than 13 percent forecast by the government, from 18.5 percent in 1996.

They said they expected higher inflation mainly because domestic consumption, seen in the 40-percent boom of credit for the non-financial sector last year, was growing quicker than the gross domestic product.

"Last year was good for the Polish economy, but not good enough to create foundations for a big leap forward which Poland needs to catch up with Western Europe," IBnGR president Janusz Dabrowski told a news conference.
"We will see a stabilisation of economic indices in the coming years," he said.

Dabrowski expected that growth in 1997 will continue to be fuelled mainly by domestic demand and investment -- whose growth rate, at nine and 18.7 percent respectively last year, should slightly fall.
Last year, the two factors replaced the expansion of exports as the main engine of Poland's economic growth.
In 1996, the exports growth rate declined to 6.1 percent, from 18.4 percent in 1995, while imports grew 20.1 percent against 22.7 percent in 1995.

The decline in exports growth was a result of weak economic performance in Western countries and of zloty appreciation. The central bank allowed the zloty to firm to contain the 1995 inflationary boom of currency reverves, Dabrowski said.
Slower growth of exports led to a widening trade deficit to more than $8 billion last year, from nearly $2 billion in 1995.

IBnGR's analyst Miroslaw Gronicki said that even though the economic recovery in the West should lift Poland's exports next year, the trade gap was still likely to rise to $14 billion and than to $15.3 billion in 1998.
He said the balooning gap would no longer be sufficiently offset by the cross-border retail trade, which brings Poland about $6 billion annually, and inflows from foreign investment.
The higher deficit may gradually cut currency reserves, puttin the zloty under depreciation pressure, he said. A weaker zloty would undermine anti-inflationary policies, he added.
"The zloty is unlikely to stay strong considering the worsening of the deficit," Granicki said. He added the dollar was likely to cost about 3.35-3.4 zlotys at the end of 1997.

He also said that meeting the 13-percent inflation target in 1997 would require much smaller than planned wage increases, especially for pensioners and public workers, which was unlikely in the year of parliamentary elections.
On the other hand, the expected high agricultural output in 1997 would help fight inflation, he said.
